# Note

Introduction to Seurat workflow

This vignette is based on [Seurat - Guided clustering tutorial](https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/pbmc3k_tutorial)

Use this vignette as a general guideline, not a ground truth.
There is no one way to analyze genomics data.
Sometimes you have to adjust your analysis based on your research question, experimental design etc.

In the future you will analyze genomic data that you or other people generated.
It is vital that, before any analysis, you familiarize yourself with the data set:

- What is the biological question you are trying to answer?
  What are the hypotheses?

- What is the study design and how was the experiment done (sample type, treatment, genetic knockout, disease, sample size, system, technology, are there any batches etc.)?

- How was the data processed (software, genome version etc.)?

- What type of data are available (raw data, count matrices, sample/cell metadata)?

Instead of just copy-pasting the code, try implementing the following logic:

1.  Read the vignette first. Try to understand each step.
2.  Without looking at the vignette, write down the main steps of the workflow (use headers to build an outline of your document at the same time). For each step, write a short comment: What is this step for?, Why is it important? Compare your answers with the vignette. It is ok if you don't remember the exact code or the name of the functions. It's more important that you understand each step conceptually.
3.  After each step write down your observations. What has changed?
4.  At the end of your analysis, think about and write down conclusions. It doesn't have to be an academic assay but try to state the main points and do a little bit of goggling.
    - Are you able to answer the initial research question and confirm/deny the hypotheses?
    - Try to connect what is known with what you have found.

The goal of this training is to help you understand the general workflow of single-cell RNA-seq analysis.
Although using AI can be beneficial and speed up your analysis, it is important that you have a good understanding of topics covered in this training and you have truly mastered the skill.
Only then you can use AI to help you with the analysis.
It is fine, to ask AI to help you with customizing a ggplot, but try not to use it for the actual analysis.

If you don't know what a function does, run `?function_name` in Console.

# About the dataset

We will use the `Crowell19_4vs4` dataset from the `muscData` package.
It is a single-cell RNA-seq experiment of the mouse brain (prefrontal cortex) from [Crowell et al.](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-19894-4).
There are 8 samples from 8 different mice: 4 were treated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a bacterial molecule that triggers an inflammatory response, and 4 with a vehicle (control).

The design makes this a good example for integration and for comparing conditions: do the cells cluster by cell type or by LPS treatment, and which genes respond to LPS in each cell type?

# Libraries

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycomm)
library(patchwork)
library(Seurat)
library(clustree)
library(readxl)
library(scuttle)
library(ggridges)
library(scDblFinder)
library(BiocParallel)
library(harmony)

```

# Import data

Data can be downloaded from [figshare](https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/On_the_discovery_of_population-specific_state_transitions_from_single-cell_RNA_sequencing_data/8976473).
Each sample is a separate library.
With the pbmc data we had only one sample so we had to create one seurat object.
Here we need to create 8 objects.

```{r}
sample_metadata <- read_xlsx("data/crowell19/metadata.xlsx")
```

```{r}
# First we have to swap genes.tsv.gz to features.tsv.gz. otherwise seurat wont read it
dirs <- list.dirs("data/crowell19", recursive = F)

for (d in dirs) {
  old <- file.path(d, "genes.tsv.gz")
  new <- file.path(d, "features.tsv.gz")
  
  if (file.exists(old) && !file.exists(new)) {
    file.rename(old, new)
  }
}
```

## Create seurat objects

Instead of copy-pasting and adjusting code for each sample individually, we're gonna be smart about and use a for loop to streamline the process.

```{r}
# 1. Get the paths for each sample
dirs <- list.dirs("data/crowell19", recursive = F)

# 2. create an empty list that will store all seurat objects
seurat_objs <- list()

# 2. Loop over dirs
for (dir in dirs){
  # Extracts the name of the last folder = sample name
  sample <- basename(dir)
  # Subset the metadata to individual sample
  sample_df <- sample_metadata[sample_metadata$`Sample ID` == sample, ]
  
  obj <- Read10X(dir)
  so <- CreateSeuratObject(obj, project = sample, min.cells = 10)
  
  # Create additional columns in metadata
  so$sample <- sample
  so$condition <- sample_df$Characteristics
  
  # add the object to the list
  seurat_objs[[sample]] <- so
}

```

```{r}
length(seurat_objs)
names(seurat_objs)
head(seurat_objs[["LC016"]]@meta.data)
head(seurat_objs[["LC017"]]@meta.data)
```

## Merging into one object

Now we have a list of 8 Seurat objects.
We can merge them into one object.
That is why we added the information to meta data at the beginning, so we are able to tell the samples apart in a merged object.

```{r}
so <- merge(x= seurat_objs[[1]], y= seurat_objs[-1], add.cell.ids = names(seurat_objs)) # x has to be a seurat obj, y can be a list of seurat objs, that's why x is the first element of the list, and y is the list without the first object
```

```{r}
so
```

After merging, the RNA assay has now 8 count layers - separate layer for each sample.

```{r}
table(so$sample)
```

The metadatas of individual seurat objects are now merged into one.

Single-cell data can take lots of memory and we should be mindful of any large objects that we don't longer need.
We can remove `seurat_objs` from the environment, because we will be using the merged one.

```{r}
rm(seurat_objs)
gc()
```

# QC and prefiltering

## MAD outliers

In the pbmc dataset we looked at the distribution of multiple metrics and determined the cutoffs.
It is easy with one sample.
Here we have 8 samples, and we can't set one threshold for all samples, because each of them has a different distribution.
We could look and individual distributions and set the thresholds manually for each sample.
For 8 samples it' already a lot, so if we had 30 samples, that would be cumbersome.

Instead of setting thresholds manually for each sample individually, we're gonna use some tricks to streamline the process.
We will use an approach that involves MAD.

**MAD** is the median absolute deviation: the median of the distances of all values from their median.
It measures how spread out the values are, like the standard deviation, but it is not pulled around by extreme values.
That matters here, because the low-quality cells we want to find are exactly the extreme values.

A cell is marked as an outlier if its value is more than a chosen number of MADs (commonly 3) away from the median of its sample:

$$\text{outlier if } |x - \text{median}(x)| > n \times \text{MAD}(x)$$

A few practical points:

- **Run it per sample.** Each sample gets its own median and MAD, so the thresholds adapt to the sample. That is what makes it work for 8 samples, or 30, without setting cutoffs by hand.
- **Use the right side.** For the number of counts and the number of genes, only low values are a problem (empty droplets, damaged cells). For the percent of mitochondrial reads, only high values are a problem (dying cells).
- **Log-transform counts and genes first.** Their distributions are skewed, so MADs work better on the log scale.
- **The number of MADs is a choice.** 3 is a common default, and 5 is more permissive. Look at the plots to check that the thresholds make sense.

First we will calculate percent mt for each cell

```{r}
so <- PercentageFeatureSet(so, pattern = '^mt-', col.name = "mito.percent") # mt - because its mouse
```

Let's first see how the distributions for each metric look like before we do anything.
I'm feeling fancy and want to make my own plots.

```{r}
multi_qc_plot <- function(seurat_obj, sample_col = 'orig.ident', metrics=c("nCount_RNA", 'nFeature_RNA', 'mito.percent') ,log_metrics = c("nCount_RNA", 'nFeature_RNA'), zoom_quantile = 0.95) {
  
  df <- seurat_obj[[]]
  plots <- list()
  
  for (metric in metrics) {
    # log10 only for the metrics listed in log_metrics (not for percentages)
    df$value <- df[[metric]]
    xlab <- metric
    zoom <- NULL
    if (metric %in% log_metrics) {
      df$value <- log2(df$value)
      xlab <- paste0("log2(", metric, ")")
    } else if (!is.null(zoom_quantile)) {
      # for metrics that are not logged, zoom in on the bulk of the cells,
      # so a long tail of outliers does not squish the distributions
      zoom <- c(min(df$value), quantile(df$value, zoom_quantile))
    }
    
    plots[[metric]] <- ggplot(df, aes(x = value, y = .data[[sample_col]], fill = .data[[sample_col]])) +
      # ndensity scales each sample to its own peak, trim stops the density at the data range
      ggridges::geom_density_ridges(stat = "density", aes(height = after_stat(ndensity)), trim = TRUE) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = median(df$value), colour = "red") +
      coord_cartesian(xlim = zoom) +
      scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Pastel2") +
      labs(x = xlab, y = NULL) +
      ggridges::theme_ridges() +
      theme(legend.position = "none")
  }
  
  return(patchwork::wrap_plots(plots))
}

```

```{r, fig.width=12, message=FALSE}
multi_qc_plot(so, log_metrics = NULL ,zoom_quantile = .99)
```

```{r}
so[[]] %>%
  group_by(sample) %>%
  summarize(
    across(
      c(nFeature_RNA, nCount_RNA, mito.percent),
      list(min = min, median = median, max = max),
      .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
    ),
    n_cells = n()
  )
```

You can clearly see that the distributions of the metrics vary a lot between the samples.
That is why we cannot inspect them together.

Let's add those MAD outliers.
We will use `isOutlier()` function from `scuttle`, that takes a metric and a batch vectors and performes per sample QC.
TRUE means that this cell is an outlier

```{r}
so$umi_outlier <- isOutlier(so$nCount_RNA, type = 'both', nmads = 3, log=T, batch = so$orig.ident)
so$ngenes_outlier <- isOutlier(so$nFeature_RNA, type = 'both', nmads = 3, log=T, batch = so$orig.ident)
so$mito_outlier <- isOutlier(so$mito.percent, type = 'higher', nmads = 3, log=F, batch = so$orig.ident)
```

We can check the actual thresholds here

```{r}
attr(isOutlier(so$nCount_RNA, nmads = 3, type = "both", batch = so$orig.ident, log = T), "thresholds")
attr(isOutlier(so$nFeature_RNA, nmads = 3, type = "both", batch = so$orig.ident, log=T), "thresholds")
attr(isOutlier(so$mito.percent, nmads = 3, type = "higher", batch = so$orig.ident,log=F),  "thresholds")
```

```{r}
table(so$umi_outlier, so$sample)
table(so$ngenes_outlier, so$sample)
table(so$mito_outlier, so$sample)
```

Most of the samples have generally low mito% with low spread.
LC020 has a higher spread.
It might just be sample specific effect that is driven by certain cell types, but it might also suggest of dying or lyzed cells.
Let's see the relationship between mito% and #genes

```{r, fig.width=20, fig.height=10}
FeatureScatter(so, "nFeature_RNA", 'mito.percent', group.by = 'mito_outlier', split.by = 'sample', ncol = 4)
```

I don't want to set a strict threshold of 5% because maybe there are cell specific to a sample where they naturally have a higher mito content.
Lots of samples are very clean so the mad cutoffs are very strict.
I going to combine MAD with a floor of 5%, so the cutoff cannot be lower than 5%.
If I see that LC020 behaves abnormally during clustering and UMAP, I can always go back and remove more cells.\

```{r}
mito_outlier <- isOutlier(so$mito.percent, nmads = 3, type = "higher", batch = so$orig.ident, log = FALSE)

# Uses 3 MADs for dirtier batches (LC019, LC020, LC025), and a 5% floor for ultra-clean batches
so$mito_outlier <- as.logical(mito_outlier) & (so$mito.percent > 5)
```

```{r, fig.width=20, fig.height=10}
FeatureScatter(so, "nFeature_RNA", 'mito.percent', group.by = 'mito_outlier', split.by = 'sample', ncol = 4)
```

```{r}
table(so$mito_outlier, so$sample)
```

## Doublet detection

A **doublet** is a droplet that captured two (or more) cells instead of one.
Its expression profile is a mix of both cells, so it can look like a new cell type that does not exist, or it can bridge two real clusters.
Doublets also tend to have more counts and more genes than single cells.

The rate of doublets increases with the number of cells loaded: for 10x data it is roughly 1% for every 1,000 cells recovered, so in a sample with 5,000 cells we expect around 5%.

Most tools work in a similar way:

1.  Simulate artificial doublets by combining the profiles of randomly chosen pairs of cells from the same sample.
2.  Place the real and the artificial cells together in a low-dimensional space (PCA).
3.  Give each real cell a doublet score, based on how many of its neighbors are artificial doublets.
4.  Call the cells with the highest scores doublets, using a threshold chosen by the tool.

Popular tools are `scDblFinder`, `DoubletFinder`, `scds` and `Scrublet`.

Things to keep in mind:

- **Run it per sample (library).** Doublets can only form between cells that were in the same droplet run, so a doublet is never a mix of cells from two different samples. Running it on the merged object would be wrong.
- **Run it before filtering.** Doublets are often removed by the count filters, and the tools need the full set of cells to simulate doublets from. The only filtering that should be applied before doublet detection is filtering out empty droplets, which cell ranger already does. But make sure to check the recommendations for the package that you're going to use.
- **It only finds some doublets.** Doublets made of two similar cells (e.g. two neurons) look like a single cell and are hard to detect. The tools are better at doublets made of two different cell types.
- **Check the result.** Look at the doublet cells on the UMAP and at their marker genes after clustering. A cluster made mostly of doublets, with markers of two cell types, can be removed.

We will use `scDblFinder`

`scDblFinder` doesn't work on Seurat object, it needs a `SingleCellExperiment` object.
Thankfully it is very easy to convert Seurat into SCE.
We need to join the count layers before we convert Seurat to SCE.
I'm gonna create a custom function to streamline the process.

```{r}
doublet_finder <- function(seurat_object, samples = "orig.ident", BPPARAM = NULL) {
  if (is.null(BPPARAM)) BPPARAM <- BiocParallel::SerialParam()
  
  seurat_object <- JoinLayers(seurat_object)
  sce <- as.SingleCellExperiment(seurat_object)
  
  # Run doublet detection (parallel if BPPARAM is a MulticoreParam/SnowParam)
  sce <- scDblFinder(sce = sce, clusters = TRUE, samples = samples, BPPARAM = BPPARAM)
  
  # Add doublet score and call to the Seurat metadata
  idx <- match(colnames(seurat_object), colnames(sce))
  doublet_score <- sce$scDblFinder.score[idx]
  doublet       <- sce$scDblFinder.class[idx] == "doublet"
  
  return(list(doublet_score = doublet_score, doublet = doublet))
}
```

```{r, eval=FALSE, }
doublets <- doublet_finder(so, samples="orig.ident", BPPARAM = BiocParallel::MulticoreParam(workers = 4))
so$doublet_score <- doublets$doublet_score
so$doublet <- doublets$doublet
```

This might take a while to run.
Import [this table](https://github.com/wiktormiko/Intro-to-genomics/blob/main/vignettes/data/crowell19/crowell_metadata_doublet_calls.csv) and extract the `doublet` and `doublet_score` columns and add to your metadata.

`data/crowell_metadata_doublet_calls.csv`

```{r}
doublets <- read.csv("data/crowell19/crowell_metadata_doublet_calls.csv")
so$doublet_score <- doublets$doublet_score
so$doublet <- doublets$doublet
```

```{r}
table(so$doublet, so$sample)
```

# Standard processing

Keep the layers split by sample

We run the regular processing, but with the per-sample count layers kept separate.
When the RNA assay has one layer per sample, `FindVariableFeatures()` is run on each layer separately and a consensus set of HVGs is then taken across samples.
This way the HVGs are not dominated by one large or batch-specific sample.
If you have joined the layers (e.g. with `JoinLayers()`), split them again by sample before this step:

``` r
so[["RNA"]] <- split(so[["RNA"]], f = so$sample)
```

```{r}
so
```

Layers are split, we don't need to do anything.

We will calculate cell cycle scores.
Seurat only provides lists for human genome, but we can convert them to mouse.
Code taken from [here](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2016/10/converting-mouse-to-human-gene-names-with-biomart-package/)

```{r}
library(babelgene)
hs2mm <- function(g) unique(orthologs(g, "mouse", human = TRUE)$symbol)

s.genes   <- intersect(hs2mm(cc.genes.updated.2019$s.genes),   rownames(so))
g2m.genes <- intersect(hs2mm(cc.genes.updated.2019$g2m.genes), rownames(so))
```

```{r, warning=FALSE}
so <- so |>
  NormalizeData(verbose = F) |> 
  CellCycleScoring(s.features = s.genes, g2m.features = g2m.genes, verbose = F) |> 
  FindVariableFeatures(verbose = F) |> 
  ScaleData(verbose = F) |> 
  RunPCA(verbose = F)
```

```{r}
ElbowPlot(so, ndims=30)
```

```{r}
so <- so |> 
  FindNeighbors(dims = 1:20, verbose = F) |> 
  FindClusters(resolution = 0.8, algorithm = 4, cluster.name = 'leiden_0.8_unintegrated', verbose = F) |> 
  RunUMAP(reduction.name = 'umap_unintegrated', dims = 1:20, verbose = F)
```

```{r, fig.width=15}
DimPlot(so, reduction = 'umap_unintegrated', group.by = c('leiden_0.8_unintegrated', 'sample', 'condition'), shuffle = T)
```

```{r, fig.width=15, fig.height=8}
DimPlot(so, reduction = 'umap_unintegrated', group.by = 'leiden_0.8_unintegrated', split.by = 'sample', ncol = 4, label = T)
```

When we look at the umap plots, although samples seem to overlap quite well, there are still some discrepancies.
Some clusters are dominated by one or two samples, one cluster still separates by condition.
Although, there might be cell types that are specific to a sample or condition, it is more likely that some clusters are not driven by cell type, but by sample/library.
The goal of clustering is that each cluster represent a cell type, not sample/library.
That's why we we often use **intergration**, when we are dealing with multiple samples/libraries/batches.

# Integration

## What is integration and why do we need it?

Cells from different samples differ for technical reasons (library prep, sequencing depth, processing day) as well as biological ones (donor, genotype, condition).
If we ignore this, cells often cluster by sample instead of by cell type, and the same cell type from two samples ends up in separate clusters.
This is the classic **batch effect**.

Integration is not only about technical batches.
Even when there is no obvious batch, e.g. every sample was prepared separately, or all were processed together, we usually still integrate.
Each sample (donor, animal, condition) is its own source of variation, and we want to line up the shared cell types across samples regardless of where the variation comes from.
Here, integration means aligning shared cell populations across samples, and it is not limited to removing technical noise.

**Integration** removes this sample-specific variation so that cells of the same type from different samples overlap in a shared low-dimensional space.
We then cluster and annotate on the integrated embedding, which makes the clusters comparable across samples.
Integration is only used for embedding, clustering and visualization.
Differential expression is still done on the original (joined) expression values, not on integrated values.

**Do we always need it?** No.
First check whether there is a problem, e.g. a UMAP coloured by sample.
If samples already mix well, integration is not needed, and too aggressive integration can remove real biology (e.g. a cell type or condition effect present in only some samples).
There are many integration method, each suited for different scenario.
Sometimes we may need a harsh integration if we, for example, re-analyze public data and want to combine samples from different studies.
Other times, our genetic knock-out or treatment may alter cell type composition and there might be a small subpopulation that is specific to one condition.
If we out integration method is too aggressive, that rare cell population might blended with with a similar cell types and we ultimately loose that condition-specific rare cell type.

### General approaches

- **Anchor-based / mutual nearest neighbours:** find pairs of similar cells across datasets and use them to correct one dataset towards another (Seurat CCA / RPCA, MNN, fastMNN).
- **Embedding correction:** leave the expression values alone and adjust the PCA coordinates so batches overlap (Harmony).
- **Probabilistic / deep learning models:** learn a latent space that is corrected for batch (scVI, scANVI).
- **Reference mapping:** project new samples onto an already annotated reference instead of integrating everything together.

### Harmony

We will use [Harmony](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-019-0619-0), which works on the PCA embedding.
It repeatedly (1) clusters the cells softly, with a penalty for clusters dominated by a single sample, and (2) computes a cluster-specific linear correction per sample and moves the cells accordingly, until the cells are well mixed.
It is fast, memory-efficient and scales to many samples.
The output is a corrected embedding (`harmony`) that replaces PCA for neighbours, clustering and UMAP.
This is why we keep the per-sample layers and run PCA first.

```{r}
so <- RunHarmony(so, group.by.vars = 'sample') # We need to specify our batches/or libraries

# We can also run:
# so <- IntegrateLayers( object = so, method = HarmonyIntegration) # It will use the sample specific layers
```

```{r}
so
```

After running harmony, we get a new reduction "harmony", we will use it instead of pca to run neighbors and umap, since harmony is basically a batch corrected pca (oversimplification :p).

```{r}
so <- so |> 
  FindNeighbors(reduction = 'harmony', dims = 1:20, verbose = F) |> 
  RunUMAP(reduction = 'harmony', dims = 1:20, verbose=F) |> 
  FindClusters(resolution = 0.8, algorithm = 4, cluster.name = 'leiden_0.8', verbose = F) 
```

We can now join the layers together, set default idents and dim.red.

```{r}
so <- JoinLayers(so)
Idents(so) <- 'leiden_0.8'
DefaultDimReduc(so) <- 'umap'
so
```

## Assessing integration

```{r, fig.width=15, fig.height=8}
p1 <- DimPlot(so, reduction = 'umap_unintegrated', group.by = c('leiden_0.8_unintegrated', 'sample', 'condition'), shuffle = T) 
p2 <- DimPlot(so, reduction = 'umap', group.by = c('leiden_0.8', 'sample', 'condition'), shuffle = T) 

p1/p2
```

```{r, fig.width=15, fig.height=8}
DimPlot(so, reduction = 'umap', group.by = 'leiden_0.8', split.by = 'sample', ncol = 4, label = T)
```

Let's plot relative contribution of each sample to clusters.

```{r}
plot_cluster_composition <- function(seurat_object, cluster_col = "seurat_clusters" ,sample_col = 'orig.ident'){
  freq <- prop.table(table(seurat_object@meta.data[[cluster_col]], seurat_object@meta.data[[sample_col]]), margin = 2)  # each sample sums to 1
  norm <- prop.table(freq, margin = 1) |> # each cluster sums to 1
    as.data.frame() |> 
    setNames(c("cluster", "sample", "prop"))
  
  ggplot(norm, aes(cluster, prop, fill = sample)) + 
    geom_col() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0, 0)) + 
    theme_void() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(), axis.title.x = element_text()) +
    scale_fill_brewer(palette = 'Set2')
  
}
```

```{r}
plot_cluster_composition(so, 'leiden_0.8')
```

# Additional QC's

## Identification of poor quality cells

Now it is a good time to go back to our QC metrics.
Sometimes a cluster doesn't represent a cell type but it consist of cells of poor quality.
Although we did prefiltering, we might have not catch all poor quality cells.
Clustering and UMAP projection can help identify those cells, because they might now cluster together.

::: callout-note
## Exercise 5

Color the UMAP (DimPlot or FeaturePlot) by different QC metrics, including mito% and cell cycle score and phase.
Are there any clusters that are driven by any of these metrics and might not represent a cell type?
:::

```{r}

```

We can also look at top marker genes for each cluster.

A cluster is likely an artifact, not a cell type, if it shows one or more of these:

- **No specific markers**.
  Few genes are expressed in most of its cells and in few cells elsewhere (high \`pct.1\`, low \`pct.2\`).

- **Markers that are ambient or low-quality genes**.
  Examples are hemoglobin (Hbb-bs, Hba-a1), Ttr, ribosomal genes (Rps/Rpl), mitochondrial genes and Gm/Rik genes (unless we expect to have blood cells).

- **Low nFeature, high mito%, or one dominating sample.** That points to damaged nuclei or ambient RNA, not biology.

Some of the mentioned genes are common in the ambient RNA of every droplet, and a nucleus with little RNA of its own is dominated by that background.
Hemoglobin usually means blood left in the tissue, since mature mouse red blood cells have no nucleus.

HVG selection, scaling, PCA, neighbors, clusters and UMAP are all calculated from the cells that were in the object at the time.
Removing cells (outliers, doublets, low-quality clusters) does not update any of them, so the results still carry the influence of the cells we removed:

- **Scaling:** the mean and variance of each gene were computed with the removed cells included.
- **HVGs:** genes that were variable only because of the removed cells (e.g. doublet or dying-cell signatures) can remain in the list, and genes that matter for the remaining cells can be missed.
- **PCA, Harmony ,neighbors, clusters, UMAP:** these were built on a graph and embedding that included the removed cells. The principal components partly reflect variation that no longer exists, and clusters can be split or merged because of them.

Normalization works on each cell independently, so technically we don't have to run it again.
Some normalization methods like SCT rely on cell composition so they need to be re-run.
We'll run `NormalizeData` again to keep our pipeline cohesive.

```{r}
# Remove the old cluster columns to keep everything clean
so$leiden_0.8_unintegrated <- NULL
so$leiden_0.8 <- NULL
# Remove umap_unintegrated to keep everything clean 
so[["umap_unintegrated"]] <- NULL
```

```{r}
# Split layers again
so[["RNA"]] <- split(so[["RNA"]], f = so$sample)
so <- so |> 
  NormalizeData(verbose = F) |> 
  FindVariableFeatures(verbose = F) |> 
  ScaleData(verbose = F) |> 
  RunPCA(verbose = F) |> 
  RunHarmony(group.by.vars = 'sample', verbose = F) |> 
  FindNeighbors(reduction = 'harmony', dims = 1:20, verbose = F) |> 
  RunUMAP(reduction = 'harmony', dims = 1:20, verbose = F) |> 
  FindClusters(resolution = 0.8, algorithm = 4, cluster.name = 'leiden_0.8') |> 
  JoinLayers()
```

## Reference based annotation

Instead of labelling clusters by hand from marker genes, we can transfer labels from an **annotated reference dataset**.
The reference can be a curated bulk or single-cell atlas of the same tissue and species.
Each cell in our data (or each cluster) is compared to the reference and gets the label of the most similar reference cells.

Common approaches:

- **Correlation-based (e.g. `SingleR`):** compares each cell's expression to reference profiles and assigns the best-matching label. It is quick and easy, with ready-made references in `celldex` (e.g. `MouseRNAseqData`, `ImmGenData`), but you can supply any annotated single-cell dataset.
- **Anchor-based label transfer (Seurat `FindTransferAnchors()` + `TransferData()`):** finds matching cells between our data and an annotated Seurat reference and transfers the labels, with a prediction score for each cell.
- **Pre-trained / web tools (e.g. Azimuth, MapMyCells):** map cells onto a published atlas.

Things to keep in mind:

- The result is only as good as the reference. It must match the species, tissue and technology, and it can only assign labels that exist in the reference. A cell type missing from the reference will be forced into the closest label.
- Check the confidence scores and drop or flag low-confidence cells instead of trusting every label. Most of the algorithms will enforce a label, instead of saying "I don't know".
- Treat the labels as a starting point. Confirm them with marker genes (e.g. dot plot or violin plots) and our clusters.

### Web-based tools

[MapMyCells](https://brain-map.org/bkp/analyze/mapmycells#taxonomies) allows users to assign cell type names from Allen Institute-hosted taxonomies to their own single cell and spatial transcriptomics data.
It.
is an online tool with several available references, focusing on both human and mouse brain tissues, so it suits well for our dataset.
It is not possible to use a custom reference, so you can't use it for anything other than brain.
There are other web-based tools though.

We need to supply a raw count matrix where rows are cells and columns are genes (csv or anndata; up to 2GB).

First, we have to convert the seurat object into h5ad (or csv)

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# BiocManager::install('anndataR')
library(anndataR)

# custom function that takes in seurat obj and strips it from everything that is not raw counts
write_simple_h5ad <- function(seurat_object, path){
  counts <- LayerData(seurat_object, assay = "RNA", layer = "counts")  
  seurat_object_min <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = counts, assay = "RNA") 
  write_h5ad(seurat_object_min, path, x_mapping = 'counts', layers_mapping=FALSE, compression = 'gzip')
}

write_simple_h5ad(so, 'crowell.h5ad')
```

Supply this file to [MapMyCells](https://knowledge.brain-map.org/mapmycells/process?refTaxonomyId=10xGene) choosing 10x Whole mouse brain as reference

```{r}
file <- "data/crowell19/crowell_10xWholeMouseBrain(CCN20230722)_HierarchicalMapping_UTC_1792284248846.csv"
map <- read.csv(file, comment.char = "#")
colnames(map)
idx <- match(colnames(so), map$cell_id)

```

Let's check the results and see whether they are trustworthy.

1.  Add all 4 levels of annotation

```{r}
for (lv in c("class", "subclass", "supertype", "cluster")) {
  so[[paste0("mmc_", lv)]]         <- map[[paste0(lv, "_name")]][idx]
  so[[paste0("mmc_", lv, "_prob")]] <- map[[paste0(lv, "_bootstrapping_probability")]][idx]
}
stopifnot(!anyNA(idx))                                   # every cell mapped
md <- as_tibble(so@meta.data, rownames='cell') |> dplyr::mutate(cluster = as.character(leiden_0.8))
```

2.  Is the mapping trustworthy

```{r, fig.height=6, fig.width=12}
sort(table(so$mmc_class), decreasing = TRUE)          
tapply(so$mmc_subclass_prob, so$leiden_0.8, median)      # confidence by cluster
VlnPlot(so, c("mmc_class_prob", "mmc_subclass_prob", "mmc_supertype_prob"), group.by = "leiden_0.8", pt.size = 0)
FeaturePlot(so, "mmc_subclass_prob") + coord_equal()                  # are low-confidence cells at borders/bridges?
```

Most cells are confident and fall into the expected classes.
Most labels are localized in clusters, they are not spread-out across multiple clusters.

3.  Summarize per cluster. We'll take most common label in each cluster.

```{r, fig.width=15, fig.height=8}
cluster_labels <- so@meta.data |>
  dplyr::count(cluster = as.character(leiden_0.8), label = mmc_subclass) |>
  dplyr::group_by(cluster) |>
  dplyr::mutate(frac = n / sum(n)) |>              # share of the cluster with this label
  dplyr::slice_max(n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

so$celltype_mmc <- cluster_labels$label[match(as.character(so$leiden_0.8), cluster_labels$cluster)]

cluster_labels
DimPlot(so, group.by = "celltype_mmc", label = TRUE, repel = TRUE)
DimPlot(so, group.by = 'celltype_manual', label=TRUE, repel=TRUE)
table(so$celltype_manual, so$celltype_mmc)    # compare with manual labels
```

I used the clustering resolution 0.8, but you should use the resolution that you have identified to be optimal (Exercise 9).
From my experience the mapping tends to be better, if the cells are slightly overclustered.
As an exercise you can try mapping on different resolutions.

### Label transfer

Label transfer uses an annotated reference Seuratobject.
It finds pairs of cells that are mutual nearest neighbors between the two datasets (the anchors), then uses those anchors to predict a label for every query cell.

Main steps:

1.  **Prepare the reference.** It should be normalized, have variable features and PCA computed, and contain a metadata column with the cell type labels.
2.  **Find anchors.** `FindTransferAnchors()` compares the query to the reference in the shared PCA space, using the genes both datasets have.
3.  **Transfer the labels.** `TransferData()` predicts a label for each query cell from its anchors, and returns a **prediction score** (0 to 1) as a measure of confidence.
4.  **Add the result to the query.** `AddMetaData()` stores the predicted labels and scores in the metadata.
5.  **Check the result.** Look at the score distribution, flag or drop low-confidence cells, and compare the labels with our clusters and marker genes.

We will use ZeiselBrainData

1.  Build the reference

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# BiocManager::install('scRNAseq')
library(scRNAseq)

zei <- ZeiselBrainData()
head(colData(zei))
ref <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = counts(zei),
                          meta.data = as.data.frame(colData(zei))[, c("level1class", "level2class")])
ref <- ref |> 
  subset(level2class != '(none)') |> 
  NormalizeData(verbose = F) |> 
  FindVariableFeatures(verbose = F) |> 
  ScaleData(verbose = F) |> 
  RunPCA(npcs = 30)
table(ref$level1class)
```

2.  Transfer labels

```{r}
anchors <- FindTransferAnchors(reference = ref, query = so, dims = 1:30, reference.reduction = "pca")

pred1 <- TransferData(anchorset = anchors, refdata = ref$level1class, dims = 1:30)
pred2 <- TransferData(anchorset = anchors, refdata = ref$level2class, dims = 1:30)

so$tf_level1 <- pred1$predicted.id
so$tf_level1_score <- pred1$prediction.score.max
so$tf_level2 <- pred2$predicted.id
so$tf_level2_score <- pred2$prediction.score.max
```

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
VlnPlot(so, c('tf_level1_score',"tf_level2_score"), group.by = "leiden_0.8", pt.size = 0)
```

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=10}
DimPlot(so, group.by = c('tf_level1',"tf_level2"), label = TRUE, repel = TRUE, shuffle = T, ncol = 1) 
```

Most cell labels are aggregated around clusters which is a good sign.

It could be difficult to make sense of the annotations if most clusters where mixture of cell types.
That could mean that our cluster might not represent cell types (we know they do in this case), the reference cell types are so similar to each other that our dataset is underpowered to tell apart (sequencing depth etc.), or that the reference dataset is not well suited for our dataset.

Similarly to MMC, we will take the most common label for each cluster as a cluster annotation.

```{r}
most_common_label <- function(seurat_obj, anno_col, cluster_col, prefix = anno_col){
  df <- seurat_obj@meta.data %>%
    dplyr::mutate(cluster = .data[[cluster_col]],
                  cell_anno = .data[[anno_col]]) %>%
    dplyr::count(cluster = as.character(cluster), label = cell_anno) |>
    dplyr::group_by(cluster) |>
    dplyr::mutate(frac = n / sum(n)) |>              # share of the cluster with this label
    dplyr::slice_max(n, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    summarise(top1      = label[1],
              top2      = label[2],
              top3      = label[3],# NA if the cluster has only one label
              frac_top1 = frac[1],
              frac_top2 = frac[2],
              frac_top3 = frac[3],
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(cluster = as.integer(cluster)) %>%
    arrange(cluster)
  return(df)
  
}
```

This table shows top3 most common labels and proportion of cells in a cluster with that label.
Some more ambiguous annotations should be investigated.
I'm going to choose the first label for the sake of the tutorial.

```{r}
top_lab_df_l1 <- most_common_label(so, 'tf_level1', 'leiden_0.8')
top_lab_df_l2 <- most_common_label(so, 'tf_level2', 'leiden_0.8')
top_lab_df_l1
top_lab_df_l2
```

```{r}
so$cell_ann_tf1 <- top_lab_df_l1$top1[match(as.character(so$leiden_0.8), top_lab_df_l1$cluster)]
so$cell_ann_tf2 <- top_lab_df_l2$top1[match(as.character(so$leiden_0.8), top_lab_df_l2$cluster)]
```

```{r, fig.height=20, fig.width=10}
DimPlot(so, group.by = c('leiden_0.8','celltype_manual','celltype_mmc','cell_ann_tf1', 'cell_ann_tf2'), label = T, repel = T, ncol = 1) 
```

```{r}
so[[]] %>%
  dplyr::select(leiden_0.8, celltype_manual, celltype_mmc, cell_ann_tf1, cell_ann_tf2) %>%
  distinct()
```

You have tried multiple methods of annotation.
It seems like a lot, but in real life we often use multiple approaches to get the most reliable annotation.
This is one of the most important steps in the whole analysis because it will dictate the results and interpretation of most downstream analyses.

# Downstream analysis

Everything so far (QC, doublet removal, normalization, integration, clustering, annotation) is a baseline.
It took a lot of work, but annotation is rarely the end of a single-cell analysis.
Once cells have labels, we can start asking the biological questions the experiment was designed for: how does each cell type respond to the treatment, which genes change, do cell type proportions shift, which pathways are involved, and what is new?

## Pseudobulk DGE

This chapter starts with the most common question, differential gene expression (DGE).

You are already familiar with bulk RNA-seq and DESeq worfklow.
You'll see that pseudobulk is extremely easy and you use what you already know!
In our DESeq tutorial we tried to compare gene expression across different conditions.
That case seemed simple, we dealt with a matrix of counts gene x sample.
In single-cell world, we have another level of complexity: genes, samples/conditions and idividual cells.
How to deal with all of this?
One of the common approaches is pseudobulk.

**What is pseudobulk?** For each cell type, we **sum the raw counts** of all cells that come from the same sample.
A genes × cells matrix becomes a genes × samples matrix per cell type (here 8 mice × \~17,000 genes).
We then test it with the statistics developed for bulk RNA-seq (edgeR, DESeq2, limma-voom).
So the only difference between bulk and pseudobulk is that in pseudobulk we have to aggregate counts from all cells across samples.
The rest of the analysis is virtually the same.

**Why not test cells directly?** Our experiment has 8 mice (4 vs 4), not \~24,000 replicates.
Cells from the same mouse share genetics, environment and handling, so they are not independent.
Treating each cell as a replicate (*pseudoreplication*) inflates confidence: methods that ignore replicate variation are biased and can report hundreds of DE genes where no biological difference exists (Squair et al. 2021).
The number of "significant" genes then follows the number of cells, not the evidence (Murphy et al. 2023).
Actually we've used a method that treats each cell as a replicate in this analysis.
`FindAllMarkers` does exactly that and the p-values are inflated.
For marker identification it's not problematic, since we focus on top markers anyways - we do not investigate all genes, especially across conditions).

**Isn't aggregation counterproductive, given single-cell resolution?** \
We loose single-cell resolution but we still keep the cell-type resolution.
We aggregate within a cell type, per mouse.
What we give up is cell-to-cell variability inside one cell type in one mouse, which doesn't answer the question "does LPS change expression?".
What we actually gain is that summing fixes sparsity.
Single-cell counts are mostly zeros.
Pooling thousands of cells gives well-behaved counts for bulk methods (Squair et al. 2021).

**What we lose.** Subpopulations responding differently within a cell type need finer clusters or a dedicated cell-level analysis.
Pseudobulk also needs enough cells per mouse per cell type, and enough mice per group.
In this dataset, clusters dominated by one mouse cannot be tested.

**Is there consensus?** Pseudobulk is the usual default (Crowell et al. 2020, the paper this dataset comes from; Squair et al. 2021).
Not everyone agrees: Zimmerman et al. 2021 argue it can be conservative and underpowered compared with mixed models.
The robust, simple choice for a first analysis is pseudobulk.

### Which cell types should be included?

A pseudobulk test compares mice, so a cell type is testable only if enough mice in both conditions contribute enough cells.

**Inclusion/exlusion rules (rules of thumb)**

1.  At least 10 cells per cell type per mouse (arbitrary number).

2.  Cell type/cluster is dominated by one replicate.
    This suggests a potential sampling issue when preparing libraries, making the results less reliable.
    It might be better to exclude that cluster

3.  Most of the replicates in each condition contribute to that cell type e.g. 3 out 4 mice.

::: callout-note
### Exercise 11

Prepare a table(s)/plots of "testable" cell types, based on the criteria above (use the granular annotation).
And write down cell types that you will use for testing.
Justify the cell types you excluded.
:::

### Aggregation

Filter the seurat object to include the cell types you'll be testing

```{r}
pb <- so
# pb <- subset(so, cell_anno_column %in% c(...))
```

Now we aggregate the counts.
I will aggregate over `cell_ann_tf1` but you should use the curated annotations

```{r}
pb <- AggregateExpression(pb, assays = "RNA", return.seurat = T,
                          group.by = c('sample',"cell_ann_tf1", "condition"))

counts <- as.matrix(pb[["RNA"]]$counts)
mtd <- pb@meta.data
```

We want to check the effect of LPS in multiple cell types.
We will run multiple different contrasts in DESeq.
e.g.

- microglia LPS vs migroglia WT

- oligodendrocytes LPS vs oligodendrocytes WT etc.

It will be easier for us if we create additional column that combines cell type and condition

```{r}
mtd$celltype_condition <- paste0(mtd$cell_ann_tf1, "_", mtd$condition)
mtd
```

### DESeq2

Now this is the part you are already familiar with!
The level of complexity is slightly higher, because there will be multiple comparisons using one dds.

::: callout-note
### Exercise 12

Run standard deseq2 preprocessing:

1.  Filtering out low count genes. It might be easier to use filter by expression from edgeR and supply your contrast.
2.  Include only protein coding genes. Exclude mitochondrial, ribosomal genes. Remember that this is mouse data. Check annotables what dataframe is used for mouse reference.
3.  Create dds with `~celltype_condition` design.
4.  Run PCA. Make sure to describe the results, e.g separation by condition, do biological reps cluster together, separation by cell type. Which factor acts stronger on sample separation: cell type or treatment? Think of potential reasons why. Is it concerning or expected? Are there any sources of variation that cannot be associated with neither treatment or cell type?
:::

To run multiple different comparisons, it would be cumbersome to copy-paste the same code and change contrast each time.
Utilize for loops (or other loop like functions)!

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# change the cell type column name accordingly
contrasts <- mtd %>%
  dplyr::distinct(cell_ann_tf1) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    contrast_name = (paste0(cell_ann_tf1, "_LPS_vs_WT")),
    contrast = purrr::map(cell_ann_tf1,
                          ~ c("celltype_condition", paste0(.x, "_LPS"), paste0(.x, "_WT")))
  )
rownames(contrasts) <- contrasts$contrast_name
contrasts
contrasts$contrast
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(DESeq2)
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(counts, mtd, design = ~celltype_condition)
dds <- DESeq(dds)
```

Generally in pseudobulk you'll get fewer DEGs, bc bulk is more powered.
That depends on particular dataset, treatment etc.
It might be better to use p.adj cutoff \< 0.1.
We can run `lfcShrink` without running results first.
We cannot then adjust parameters such as alpha (0.1 by default), which is fine because we use our custom filtering functions anyways.

You can use lapply to convert the results to df, and apply your custom function (to have diffexpr column etc).

```{r, eval=FALSE}
res_list <- map(contrasts$contrast,
                ~ lfcShrink(dds, contrast = .x, type = "ashr")) 
names(res_list) <- contrasts$contrast_name
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
lapply(res_list, summary)
```

You can use lapply to convert the results to df, and apply your custom function (to have diffexpr column etc).

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# res_list <- lapply(res_list, your function, additional parameters if necessary)
```
